How I feel about viewing people as clothing loot

Honestly, I'm not sure how I feel about that.

On the one hand, it seems great, since no matter how serious or casual of a playthrough, this does seem to mean that you don't have to make sacrifices to invest in fun and silly things.

On the other hand, I'm concerned about enemy scaling. If things are scaled too mildly, being able to level a legion just by quietly coughing somewhere in the same zipcode as them will make things boring....but, if it's too aggressive and enemies grow too quickly, that'll defeat the whole "do whatever you like!" nature of such a system.

Maybe this will finally give Bethesda a reason to fix enemy scaling? I doubt it though. From the tweet what it sounds like is that there will be a level cap for the game, but that after you beat the main quest line the cap gets lifted.

Well... I guess, that's one way to ensure that whatever the final boss is, that you don't get so over-powered that you basically become Thor and can level him just by shifting your tightened buttocks.

Still, I'm also hopeful that Bethesda will work on the enemy scaling...though, I also share your skepticism.

If nothing else, though, having a far more modern game will create all sorts of amazing modding capabilities, so... At least yay for that.

I agree this is not necessarily a good thing.

It implies that levelling is sort of pointless, although I think that probably means that perks are nerfed more than enemy scaling is buffed, but it's probably both.

I mean, it wouldn't necessarily be so bad if (and only if) Bethesda fixed the enemy scaling, but... Eh. I do hope that the game is fantastic when it finally drops...though, I can't say that I'm holding my breath too much.

I personally hate level scaling, the real joy of earlier fallout/rpgs was that at the start all enemies could fuck you up and you have to be careful. Then you get to a point where there are still areas you have to avoid and then one day you get the joy of becoming a bad ass.

Fallout 3 and NV (the deathclaws and cazadors in nv aside) I felt like badass from the start and then kind of got slightly more badass towards the game but not that much because of level scaling.

I remember playing nv and deciding to start as a weak combat female who would talk her way out of things and sneak around. One situation left me surrounded by 4 guys and no melee skill and only a butchers knife. I was about to reload but I thought I'd see how it played out. I slaughtered the lot with a melee skill of 9?

Having no cap allows the really casual to complete the game if they are willing to work and allows the rest of us to enjoy the god likeness at the end of the game a lot of us crave. Those of us who really want to challenge yourselves will be smart enough to find a way. Maybe as simply as limiting the side quests you do on first play through to refusing to use points on certain things to restrict your character to a build.

Yeah so I'm happy about no level cap.

Maybe, it's because it took me a while to adjust to the game, but... I still remember my first serious combat encounter in Fallout 3 on my first playthrough, as I had started out rough. It was outside of the Super-Duper Mart against three raiders that I had barely survived with no ammo and minimal health, having to carefully sneak my way back to Megaton...and, that made coming back and clearing out the area several hours later THAT much more satisfying.

Yeah, I suppose, that can be an interesting way to challenge yourself. It's kind of like an intentional version of what I had done in Skyrim, after finding out about the ability to make skills go legendary...where, as a level 16 (or, thereabouts), I had got sick of not having points to invest in skills, so I found a corner, where I made Sneak go legendary twenty times....and, having only THEN thought about the consequences of me having my overall level skyrocket, I suddenly found that surviving started being a far more fascinating challenge.
I'm pretty sure there's a difficulty bar for consoles or people who just like to take it easy, make the game casual or challenging.

My concern isn't the slider itself, as I'm sure it'll be around, but how it will affect the enemies and what stats it will alter on what scale, as there is a rather fine line between "challengingly satisfying" and "tedious".

I'm guessing it changes stats like DT and/or skills. It shouldn't change the equipment anyone's carrying as that would be an easy way to get OP gear in the beginning. Skyrim rules you'd also get more xp with difficult enemies, but I think that's a bad idea for FO.

I'm a bit concerned about just how much Fo4 will inherit from Skyrim (e.g. Those vile skill trees), though... I suppose, at this point, speculation without experience won't do too much good.

That being said, with the game being built on a far more modern foundation, even if the vanilla scaling is rubbish, I'm sure that the community will find a way to remedy that. So... Yay.

Should [Pennsylvania] sentencing be based on crimes that haven't been committed yet? PA might use 'precrime' style algorithms to aid sentencing

Depends on what criteria are being used to determine risk level, really. I'm generally in favor of keeping non-violent people out of prison, because putting them behind bars is costly to everyone. It makes it difficult to keep family ties strong, makes it impossible for the convicted person to keep a job, and it's really hard for people to readjust to the outside after being incarcerated for years.

From the piece: "Fosque is quick to talk about drinking and the life choices that landed him in jail. But he also feels he owns the responsibility and effort it has taken to stay sober. He hadn’t heard of risk assessment, but after he was told that the tools were used to determine which facility he served time in and what level of supervision he received on parole, he looked them up online. “You mean to tell me they’re using statistics to determine what’s going to happen to me?” he asked. “That ain’t right.”"

Statistics is used to determine the rate you pay for car insurance, homeowners insurance, etc. Credit companies use knowledge of what stores you patronize to determine your financial situation: if you suddenly start using your card at Family Dollar and TJ Maxx when you had been using it at Nieman Marcus previously, they may drop your credit line because they're worried you may have lost your job. You're creating a data trail every time you do anything, and with "Big Data" companies are allowed to leverage that information to determine your risk level.
